questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That I could improve my language skills and experience a new health care system with the goal of maybe moving abroad after my studies.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Heidelberg is absolutely amazing and the city is perfect for an exchange! I've made some great friends and had lots of good experiences and would do it all again. BUT if you are a medical student coming from Denmark the clinical/academic part is extremely disappointing.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: You get an enormous amount of emails with information. Of course it's better with a little too much information, but it was also very hard to sort between what was need to know and nice to know.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Absolutely non. The key to my room could only be picked up before 5 pm which wasn't very accommodating to those of us arriving with train from afar. Also there was no orientation days for medical students as we were in the clinic. As replacement there was however a little online meeting that was announced two days before it took place and did not accommodate that we where in the clinic from 12-20...

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Typical dorms with studios and flat shares

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Depending on the apartment there's a hob and maybe an oven. I lived in a flat share and the fridge is very small so you typically have one shelf and also there is basically no freezer. My roommates had utensils that I luckily could borrow, but if you live in a studio the kitchen will be totally empty.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The housing is cheap but also pretty worn down.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didn't have to register as my courses (clinical rotations) where already decided by my home university.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't know as I didn't register. But I heard from others that it was pretty confusing to register as the process can vary from course to course and professor to professor.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Seemed like there wasn't really any help offered.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As mentioned I didn't have to register.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think most people showed up at the professors Sprechstunde and registered that way.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The academic programme was, and this is no understatement, absolutely terrible. The first day we showed up at the emergency room for internal medicine they didn't know that we were coming. We waited for two hours before a doctor asked us who we were and asked us if we had uniforms which we didn't as all we had received at this point was an email stating where to show up. She then sent us home saying she would make sure to get us uniforms for the next day. When we showed up the next day that was although not the case and we had to sit in our own clothes with the coat we brought from home over it. At no point were we welcomed, introduced to what was the function of the department or shown around. We had to use the patients toilet as we didn't get a key for the staff bathroom. We couldn't even open the door to the kitchen as we didn't have an employee card (which we asked for and were told that they didn't really want to bother getting us one for five weeks). This also meant that we had to change in the patient bathroom as we couldn't access the changing room . Also we could only change in to uniforms as I found out on my own how to get my student card registered so that I could get uniforms - if I hadn't I would have had to wear my civil clothes all five weeks. Anyways, we then showed the doctor our logbook with the clinical skills we were supposed to practice. But in the five weeks we almost exclusively took a few histories and were basically did not receive any kind of feedback (it seemed more like a way to get rid of us). Once when I said something wrong one doctor even laughed at me. When we asked if we could go talk to a patient or follow them to a procedure we were almost always told that we couldn't. We were although good enough to be used to transport patients to scans and the overnight station. Also the doctor decided for no apparent reason that we had to be there from 12-20 instead of during day time. We had no say in this. At the end of the stay she also just signed basically all of the things in our logbook even though we had practiced basically non of the skills. 
We then changed to visceral surgery where we at least got an employee card so we could access the changing room and go to the toilet. But once again I showed up at the station (E1) where no one knew who I was and clearly had absolutely no interest in finding out. I was then told to follow a PJ-student and then he could introduce me to the station. He was really nice and did a great job! But what he did (and therefore what I did) was basically do blood work and insert peripheral cannulas and then present the incoming patients at the afternoon conference. Preparing the patients for conference required that I had access to the computer system which I of course wasn't allowed to have? Therefore I had to walk from computer to computer to see if someone was logged in so I could use their account (until they had to use it again and I again would have to look for a new one). In the beginning I got to carry a phone so I could get called to do blood work/cannulas and sometimes get called to assist in the OR. This was so to more like a job and not at all a learning experience. When I went to the OR I did though get to see a little bit of surgery (while holding a retractor for hours) and most of the time the operators were actually also nice and sometimes even explained what they were doing. But after two weeks three new PJ-students came to the station and the one doctor directly told me that I had to give up the phone as they were way more important than me and needed to be prioritized over me. This of course made me feel even more welcome at the station... At the end the situation was the same with the logbook being signed even though I had done basically nothing of the things noted in there.
In the end we had two weeks in anesthesia department at the kopfklinik. Here people also had no clue who we were. But for the first time the assistent doctors actually showed a tiny interest in us and I actually learned something being there which was a huge improvement in comparison to the previous ten weeks. Here we also got to attend the classes for PJ-students which was actually quite good.
So all in all there was absolutely no program for us exchange students and I rather had the feeling that it was expected that we were just supposed to be happy that we got to be at "the famous University Clinic of Heidelberg".

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Well we didn't have courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Hard to compare as there wasn't any teaching...

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
5 weeks of rotations in internal medicine
5 weeks of rotations in visceral surgery
2 weeks of rotations in anesthesia

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I heard from other students who followed normal courses that they were quite good so would definitely recommend doing those instead of rotations!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The university offers really cheap sport classes/activities!
A big part of the city consists of students who just moved there and therefore are seeking new friends. This means that there are a lot of events and social opportunities!!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: In the beginning I went to the ESN-events to meet other students, but this is mostly internationals. To meet "locals" I would definitely recommend joining a sport, reading club or orchestra (just anything that you find interesting).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The city itself is lovely. Was only there for four months, but would have loved to see more of the surroundings.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy - German and Danish culture are quite similar.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: See above

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It's not normal to be friendly/familiar with patients and as a non native speaker it's hard to remember to use the "Sie".

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: In comparison to Danes the Germans have a great work ethic and I find that in general people were very friendly!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Don't go if you want a good academic output
2) Go if it's more important to explore the lovely city
3) Go if you want to develop personally and not academically

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: That I know that I can survive any clinical rotation.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Well I think my previous answers speak for themselves.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
